analysis.body:
Per GAO, federal AI adoption is early and uneven. Twenty of 23 agencies reported about 1,200 current and planned AI use cases, while three agencies reported not having uses for AI. Most of the reported AI use cases were in the planning phase and not yet in production; in about 200 instances, agencies reported that they were currently using AI. NASA and Commerce reported the highest number of AI use cases.

The uses GAO catalogued include analyzing data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, analyzing photographs from drones, targeting of scientific specimens for planetary rovers, identifying information security threats, and facilitating the review of large datasets. These are operational and analytical applications drawn from agency inventories.

The only money figure in these sources is the President's fiscal year 2023 budget request, which included $1.8 billion for nondefense research and development investment in AI. Institutional capacity is uneven: Commerce created a plan to develop AI technical standards and GSA established the AI Center of Excellence, while OMB has not yet developed guidance for the acquisition and use of AI and OPM has not yet established or updated an occupational category for those employees performing AI work.

ROI evidence is not reported in these excerpts. GAO states that AI could improve government operations, but the report focuses on inventory completeness and compliance rather than measured cost savings or performance gains. The sources do not provide a return-on-investment figure for government AI deployments.

Risks and regulatory posture are the dominant theme. GAO found that federal law and guidance have several requirements for agencies implementing AI, but they haven't all been met; there's no government-wide guidance on how agencies should acquire and use AI. Ten of 23 agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, 12 implemented some but not all, and one was exempt. Five agencies provided comprehensive information for each of their reported use cases while the other 15 had instances of incomplete and inaccurate data, and two inventories included AI uses that were later determined by the agencies to not be AI. GAO warns that AI poses risks that can negatively impact individuals, groups, organizations, communities, and society, and that without accurate inventories, the government's management of its use of AI will be hindered.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy in government, the record shows a government still building the management layer around AI. OECD.AI gives access to 900+ national AI policies and initiatives, and in July 2024 the GPAI initiative and OECD member countries' work on AI joined forces under the GPAI brand to create an integrated partnership. Oxford Insights' Government AI Readiness Index scores nearly every country on policy capacity, governance, infrastructure, and public-sector adoption. The AI Laws section on theworldofai.org tracks 2,425 state AI bills and the federal register watch live, and Stanford HAI's annual AI Index carries the government and policy track covering legislation counts, national strategy execution, and public-sector procurement. The takeaway is that adoption is real but mostly in planning, and compliance with inventory and risk requirements is incomplete.

https://oecd.ai/.brief: OECD.AI is a policy observatory that maintains a database of over 900 national AI policies and initiatives, alongside live AI data and policy analysis. The platform promotes the OECD AI Principles to help countries develop trustworthy AI systems, and invites organisations developing advanced AI to submit reports on their risk mitigation measures to improve transparency and comparability. In July 2024, the GPAI initiative merged with OECD member countries' AI work under the GPAI brand to form an integrated partnership. The observatory aims to support AI actors in building systems that respect human rights, fairness, transparency, explainability, robustness, and security.

https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-1059.brief: GAO reported that federal agencies have begun implementing AI, which is defined as computing systems that “learn” how to improve their performance, but many policy requirements remain unmet. Twenty of 23 agencies listed about 1,200 AI use cases, most still in planning and only roughly 200 in production, and inventories often omitted required data such as life-cycle stage or releasability. While Commerce and the GSA fully met selected requirements, agencies like OMB, OPM, and OSTP did not, and only ten agencies met all their AI requirements, twelve met some, and one was exempt. The report notes that AI can improve government operations but also poses risks, and the FY 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for non-defense AI R&D.
